item.content:encoded:
I believe strongly in the importance of bringing the perspectives and wisdom of survivors to the broader community, as I do in the Survivors’ Voices posts on this blog.

However, I also recognize that this blog is just words on a screen. Sometimes it’s hard to know whether it’s making any difference.

The place I know we’re making a difference? Awake’s concrete, personal ministry to abuse survivors, especially at our annual retreat.

(Just FYI, in case you’re new to this blog - I’m the executive director of a nonprofit organization called Awake. In Spirit and Truth is just a little side project. You can learn more about Awake at www.awakecommunity.org, and sign our Letter to Survivors here.)

For the past four years, Awake has offered a beautiful weekend retreat for those who have experienced sexual abuse by a Catholic leader, and this summer we expanded to two retreats to meet the growing interest in this opportunity for community, support, prayer, and renewal. Here are some powerful words from Patty, one of our participants:

“I had come to the retreat believing I was alone. I came carrying shame. I came carrying guilt. I came believing that no one could really understand my experience.

What I discovered was exactly the opposite. I discovered that I was not alone. I discovered that others understood in ways I never imagined. I discovered that the shame and guilt I had carried for so long did not belong to me. Most importantly, I discovered that healing happens in community.

As I left that first retreat, I wasn’t suddenly healed, and all my questions weren’t answered. But I left with something I hadn’t had when I arrived: hope.”

We have 20 survivors coming for our second retreat August 7-9, and we are in the midst of a fundraising campaign that allows us to offer this retreat free for all participants.

Would you consider making a donation to support this retreat? You can learn more at this link.

Make a Gift Here

Thank you so much for considering this! Please let me know if you have any questions.

Whether or not you are not able to make a financial gift, your prayers would also be greatly appreciated.

With gratitude,
Sara

item.title: Survivors' Voices: Isolation, Part 2
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson

item.content:encoded:
This topic resonated deeply with many on the Survivors’ Voices panel, reminding me that isolation is a heartbreakingly common consequence of abuse. At the same time, I’m encouraged that many survivors have eventually found their way back to connection and community. I’m grateful to be a small part of that through Awake.

(In case you missed it, you can read Part One of this post here.)

  • I think isolation is one of the hardest impacts of the abuse I experienced. It can feel like falling into a deep, dark pit. You can never seem to get your footing and all around you is dark and unknown. My abusers made sure I was isolated from any sort of support or care. This isolation fed into this underlying belief that I was wearing some sort of human repellent and that there is something intrinsically wrong with who I am. Even to this day, these lies weave themselves into all my relationships and the way I view myself and the world. This only serves to increase the profound feelings of loneliness and isolation. I know one of the ways to combat isolation is through vulnerability and community, but that often feels like an impossible task. It is hard to allow people close to me when my trust has been fundamentally betrayed many times in my life.

  • There have been literally YEARS where isolation was my middle name. I’m talking shades drawn, hiding in bed, interacting or communicating only when absolutely necessary or forced. Those were the very early days of my breakdown and especially once the graphic memories surfaced, in my 60’s. The world was at best, disorienting and at worst, terrifying. I’ve come a long way since then. Therapy and especially survivor groups were able to give me my life back. Being in survivor groups with people who “get” me opened me up. I was able to unfreeze from my isolation, begin to explore the overwhelming confusion and painful feelings, and find kindness, compassion and mutual friendships, some of which have lasted for over a decade now. There were years when I was attending 10 to 15 survivor groups a month. They sustained me and helped me grow. Hearing how so many others had been through almost identical experiences was very validating. Groups expanded my ability to benefit from therapy, too. I have grown and healed in ways I never imagined, and have progressed to the point of being able to be of service to others who are in the early stages of their healing journey.

  • I self-isolated after my abuse began when I was seven. Knowing what I know now, I was a perfect target. The simple hugs and attention quickly turned into abuse. Then I stayed away from people, so that I did not give others the opportunity to abuse me. I felt shame and didn’t understand what was happening. I wondered, “If people, including my family, found out what was happening, what would they think of me?” and “What did I do wrong?”. I never told anyone until my late twenties. Until I reported my abuse around ten years ago, I had only told five people. I now absolutely enjoy being around others, yet I would consider my main personality as that of a loner.

  • In any crowd. In any room. It is always that thing that can’t be talked about. When I have, I was immediately labelled. “You are one of those people. Do you know how many false reports there?” “How do I know that you won’t falsely report me?” “We all know those people are Church haters. They’re just in it for the money.” When you can’t talk about the truth of your lived experience, it takes a heavy toll. You are always unseen. You have to focus your energy on how to “fit in.” This means that you never truly belong. The truth does not go away, just because it is inconvenient to those around us. Healing doesn’t come, because healing requires the truth. As long as the Catholic Church leadership prefers their comfort to the truth and reality of the situation, the Church’s mission of healing will be unfulfilled. They continue to drive souls away from God and his grace through his established means.

  • I used to feel very isolated in relation to this abuse. And since I got such a negative response from the clergy in my diocese, I wrapped myself up in an imaginary blanket and dealt with my feelings alone. Since I’ve been a part of Awake, especially after meeting other survivors on retreat, I don’t feel so isolated and alone. I’ve found people to share this experience with and it has helped me open up this place in myself. It’s helped me move towards some profound healing. The injury is still there but I don’t feel alone like I used to.

  • What I desire now is to give my days more life and presence. God’s work with me has been long and arduous, as I have been stubbornly clinging to habits of self-protection that, at this age, are no longer potent. Distilling the grief of victim into a potion of grit and grace stirs the desire for action within me - to extend a hand of hope and the belief that dignity can be restored, that the right to be seen and our abuse acknowledged as legitimate and egregious is essential to owning ourselves as deserving of respect and dignity. The choices I now make in my life matter. The thoughts I believe now - protracted isolation or viable visibility -matter. I choose witness not withdrawal.

  • I have habitually gone through this life faking presence in interpersonal and social situations. It is too risky to again expose my spirit to the devastation of heartbreak, betrayal and rejection. Isolation is not an ideal way to live, but I became attached to the concept that if I isolate, I can disappear in a smoke and mirror existence, be seen socially as superficial and without emotional depth and therefore, uninteresting. Boring was a beautiful state of security for me. I also determined that if I don’t trust, if I close my heart, then I appear to hold nothing of value for a prospective demon predator to again defile and render me a victim.

    That said, this illusion of invisibility that I have held can no longer deny the truth that I am visible to others and they are not repulsed by my existence. The Awake community has literally awakened me to connection. I am not the only one to have been crushed by unspeakable cruelty and malignant selfishness, nor is what happened to me so unique or horrifying that I must be labeled a social leper. I am cautiously optimistic that at the end of this life, I can experience what it means to be valued and feel a sense of worth even in my brokenness.

  • I would say that my isolation has changed over time. I am now very comfortable around people. I do not feel guarded and watching everything I say. I will say that the discussion of abuse does not often enter into general conversation. I do watch and choose who I share my journey through abuse with. More often than not, it is someone struggling in some way - be it abuse, addiction, anxiety, or something else. I have no difficulty sharing and supporting someone else looking for support in their journey of life. What was such a difficult, isolating, and even painful time in some way has become a blessing, because I am able to journey with others. I would never wish the abuse on anyone, butI do know that it is only by the grace of God that I am here.

  • Isolation has been a prominent feature of my post-abuse experience. In the confessional and in pastoral counseling, my parish priest was very loving and supportive. In the parish at large though, abuse remains invisible, and I suspect that my priest is deeply uncomfortable helping the congregation grapple with the fact that abuse has been part of the church landscape for a long time. I was grateful for the one time it was mentioned in the prayers of the faithful, but that was one time in six years. I also think that some of our ideas of what holiness looks like in the church at large - holiness as outward observances, devotions, right answers - continue to allow abuse to fester invisibly. I am grateful to spaces like this that let me tell my story and feel less alone.

Thank you for reading and for caring. Perhaps this might be a good moment to consider what you can do to help someone in your life feel a little less alone.

With gratitude,
Sara

PS: Please watch for an update next month on some exciting changes coming for this blog!

Please consider sharing this post to help more people listen and learn from the experiences of survivors.

Share

item.title: Survivors' Voices: Isolation
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson

item.content:encoded:
One of the threads I have seen running through many survivors’ stories is the experience of isolation - a sense of loneliness that can persist even in the company of others. I am grateful to all the members of the Survivors’ Voice Panel who offered their reflections on this theme in their own life.

  • I’ve learned not to talk about my story in person. My family and a few close friends know, but I quickly figured out that sharing it with anyone else results in a shocked silence and immediate subject change. I’m still in the Church, but I’ve come to the conclusion that in-person spiritual advice from a priest is probably permanently off the table- not only because I have trust issues, but because I’m fairly certain they wouldn’t know what to do with me. I wouldn’t say I’m isolated, I still live in community with others, but there’s a part of me that I don’t share, and I do feel cut off from “normal” Catholic life in some ways.

  • The isolation I experienced was orchestrated by my then-husband, eventually with the support of his second wife and my biological sibling. The abuse - which was framed by them as my debauchery - isolated me from all but one person (there was a second, who, years later, returned to me). The isolation cost me nearly everything. However, eventually I rebuilt. (Long story very short.) All these years later, my life now is rich, yet I still struggle with fears that they will do this again, here, 700 miles away. Therapy helps, but the holes in my history, resulting from that isolation, will always be there.

  • I try to combat my feelings of isolation due to the painful abuse imposed upon me when I was a child, by acknowledging that all people carry some painful past or tragic loss in their hearts that still deeply affects them today. Sharing my story with people I trust is important and helps to reduce feeling isolated. Also, the stories of others who suffered from any trauma or loss are important too. I feel sharing stories together helps to break the cycle of isolation and not allow our traumatic past to define our futures.

  • The abuse violently ejected me from my parish faith community. As a stay-at-home mom whose primary social life was through the parish, this was devastating. I felt like I had to have a double life to continue to practice my faith. Everybody around me loved the pastor, and I knew what an evil, deceiving, selfish man he was. I felt stuck, like inside an invisible prison, going through the motions alone without connection.

  • I often feel isolation. Part of that is my problem with connecting to a protective social circle. I’ve progressed pretty well on my healing. I like to express myself with a bold dignity, which sometimes makes me not acceptable to many people.

  • My family and I had become close friends and even associate members of the abuser's religious order. I tried talking to a couple of friends within the order about what had happened. Their responses were all willful blindness, something that my abuser had carefully indoctrinated into everyone around him. They all said, "Oh, that's just the way he is. He's relational and needs to be with people." Father Abuser spent time alone with vulnerable women regularly, and he was very close to two religious sisters in the community who fostered children. He spent a lot of time with the children. Everyone knew. The signs of abuse were all around us, and everyone I knew in the community sacrificed their friendships with me to remain in denial. It was basically the same with the diocese. I felt like I was alone on an island in the middle of the ocean where I could see ships passing on the horizon, but no help would come.

  • The memory of my abuse was repressed for 60 years. For all that time, I wasn't able to make professional connections or strong emotional connections. I'm now 73 and I feel deep sadness to know there are many things that I'll never be able to have. I often feel excluded and rejected.

  • My husband, who was ultimately supportive, was absolutely mystified by what I told him. He couldn’t wrap his mind around having had someone who we considered so close to the family betray us. It took months for him to begin to understand the depth of deception that had taken place. That was probably the most isolating part, those months alone with the truth when my husband and children were grappling with the loss of someone we considered a close friend and pastor.

Thank you for reading. I’ll have more reflections on this topic next month.

~ Sara

Please consider sharing this post to help more people listen and learn.

Share

item.dc:creator: Sara Larson

What I learned from that poll is that many of you really appreciate both the Survivors’ Voices posts and the Reading Roundup, and you wo…
item.content:encoded:
Hi friends,

You may have noticed that I haven’t published a Reading Roundup for a while. (Since February, actually.) So, I thought I should explain.

If you’ve been following this blog over the past year, you know how busy I have become with the work of Awake, and you saw the reader poll I put out a few months ago to help me discern the direction of this blog. What I learned from that poll is that many of you really appreciate both the Survivors’ Voices posts and the Reading Roundup, and you would like me to continue both. I agree that both serve an important role in helping us be informed (myself just as much as anyone), and it has been hard for me to think about letting go of either piece.

However, the last few months have been crazy busy with conferences, speaking engagements, travel, training a new employee, illness, and my daughter’s college graduation. I didn’t exactly make a decision to pause the Reading Roundups, I just got so hopelessly behind that I could not get a post up for March, which became April and then May.

I made a promise to myself that this summer I would spend less time working at my computer and more time enjoying the beautiful outdoors here in Wisconsin. So, I think that I need to let go of “catching up” and just put this feature on hold for now. I may come back to it in a few months, or I may set it aside for good. I’m not sure yet. I’m trying to find the right balance for my life, and I appreciate all of you who have encouraged me to take care of myself in the midst of the heavy work I do.

If it’s important to you to continue following the news regarding abuse in the Church, I hope you will find other ways to do so. Setting up a weekly Google alert for the words “Catholic abuse” is one possibility, and the “abuse tracker” feed at Bishop Accountability compiles many of the most important articles (it’s just a long list to wade through). Much of the best investigative journalism on this topic is happening at The Pillar and The Guardian, but there are great articles coming out from many other outlets as well (which is why I created this feature to begin with!).

Thank you for caring about this. It matters.

Peace,
Sara

PS: I will have a Survivors’ Voices post for you later this month, on the topic of isolation. I’m looking forward to hearing what our panelists have to say.

item.title: Survivors' Voices: What I Would Say to My Abuser, Part 2
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson

item.content:encoded:
If you’ve been reading In Spirit and Truth for a while, this should be obvious by now. But I’ll say it here, just in case we need a reminder:

Each survivor is unique. Their stories, reactions, journeys, and perspectives are as varied as in any other group of human beings. That’s a big part of why I put together this Survivors’ Voices series - so that hearing from a diverse group of survivors would break down stereotypes and assumptions we might have about “what survivors are like” or “how survivors think.”

The responses to this topic are a clear demonstration of that variety and diversity. I hope they give you a small peak into the complex reality of those who have experienced abuse in the Church.

(In case you missed it, you can find the first post on this topic here: What I Would Say to My Abuser, Part 1.)

  • I would like to tell the abuser that he did not win! God sees all things and God will prevail and will heal those who were victimized by him. God will restore my dignity. I now have more courage and strength to help others prevent clergy abuse from happening ever again.

  • You looked for vulnerability. And you found that in me. Your preyed on that vulnerability to inflict even more harm. Previous to knowing you, the Church was the one place I thought of as safe. Because of you, I lost that. I no longer feel safe in Church. It has taken a lot of effort to try to calm my nervous system. To try to function in the space again. I lean heavily on God, because the Church hierarchy has failed me repeatedly. I recognize there will never be justice in this life. We don't have leaders who believe in what the Church teaches. And we certainly don't have ones with the courage to live it.

  • I read this month’s topic, and once I got past a bunch of F-bombs to which I defaulted, I knew/felt/realized that this question is predicated on the condition that the person who abused me listen. And I KNOW that he never would. Even back then, 25 years ago, he completely rewrote the narrative, broadcast it, and let me know that he did so and what others said in response - until I went no contact. I realize people change. However, looking at what he is doing with respect to speaking engagements, etc., I see no evidence that he has deviated from behaviors that could be described as narcissistic, self-serving, wholly self-unaware, and self-protective. I wouldn’t waste my breath.

  • It has been 50+ years since the events. I harbor no anger any longer, only a profound sadness for the individual that was so harmed, so pathological and so unable to treat other human beings in even a semi-normal way. His reign of abuse may have started with me, but he evolved into a serial abuser who went so far as to traffic vulnerable women from the Philippines as his own sex toys. I am blessed to have been at the beginning of his abuses and have recovered well thanks to a lot of wonderful people. What would I say to him? “I am overwhelmingly sorry for whatever happened in your life that caused such damage that it led you to act in such heinous ways. The pain you suffered must have been horrific. I sincerely hope, in death, that you have found peace.”

  • Writing out what I wish my abusers knew… there’s an undercurrent of rage at them that I’ve never really experienced or felt before—never *let* myself experience or feel before—and that I can’t even let myself fully feel now. I want to make them hurt. I’m so angry at their manipulation and abuse and gaslighting and how they pretended to be innocent and to know everything—including pretending to know everything about *me*—and how they made me feel so ashamed and so *stupid* and so incompetent—things I still feel and believe today. I … perhaps … wish they’d go to hell for what they did. I can’t stomach the thought of ever seeing or being around them again. It’s been almost 12 years and they still show up in my dreams (nightmares) sometimes, while I am sure they barely remember me, if they remember me at all. Everything is so, so backwards and unfair. Why do I have to carry the burden and the spiritual, emotional, and physical scars of what they did while they get off scot-free? Why do I have to hurt while they don’t?

  • I hope for your sake that you owned up to someone about this. But since you lied to me and to the nuncio it seems unlikely that you would. I know that the Lord says to forgive and so I choose to forgive, even if you do not deserve forgiveness for all the pain you have caused in my life. But forgiveness is an ongoing thing, and sometimes I need to forgive you every day. Do you think of the lives you wreaked havoc in every day?

  • The abuse went on for several years and involved multiple priests. Because I was split into several “inner children” due to the intensity of the abuse, I have many “opinions” floating inside me. Some of my inner children want to shame their abusers with deeply cutting comments about the pain they caused and the fact that there is no excuse for what they did. Others want to find forgiveness in their hearts because they can’t believe anyone could do something so horrendous unless they, too, must have been abused. Some have so much residual anger that they have no words – they want to burn the church down with the perpetrator trapped inside. And then there are those who want to ask them, “what would possess you to hurt me like that?!?” They want answers. They want to make sense of what happened. Some would simply melt down and sob and let the perpetrator see firsthand the destruction they caused. And some would cower in fear because they are still re-living the terrors and could never feel safe in their presence. One decided she would simply bring Jesus with her and watch how the criminal priest would react to Jesus’s presence, and His request for an explanation. That was my favorite.

  • I should thank you, Father. Your abuse burned my faith to the ground until there was nothing but ashes. I, and the merciful Lord, have had to rebuild it. I am stronger, more mature in my faith, and planted firmly on the stone foundation of a God with big shoulders who can take my anger, my accusations, my pain, my doubts, my despair, and still love. I heard this translation of Psalm 23 that describes my journey. "Surely [God's] goodness and kindness will pursue me all the days of my life" (verse 6a). When I have turned my back, He follows me calling my name. Before you, Father, I thought God was someone I could never please. Without you I don't know if I would have ever learned what a loving, true, invincible, protecting avenger God we have.

  • Death would be too good a punishment for your abuse. I think about restorative justice and my abuse by you as an adult and all the people I saw you grooming, including foster children. Since you were ordained almost 40 years ago, I suspect your victims number in the hundreds. How can there be restorative justice, in human terms, for that much debauchery? Your superior, my family friend, who said, “I think you’re wrong. You’re misinterpreting,” when I reported you deserves public humiliation and be stripped of his priesthood. You are both unfit to be publicly acknowledged as men of any honor.

  • Father Abuser, I want you to know that any time an opportunity opens for me to tell my truth, I will. I will never stop. “The truth is like a lion; you don’t have to defend it. Let it loose and it will defend itself.” - St. Augustine

  • When I had the opportunity to speak directly to the priest who abused me, I entered hoping to be heard and to speak honestly about the harm done. In retrospect, I wish the meeting had taken place on neutral ground rather than within the friars’ cloistered space, as the setting created an imbalance and made it difficult to feel fully supported. Before the meeting began, he approached me alone and initiated an unsolicited hug, which felt inappropriate and unsettling. During our conversation, he appeared to listen but did not acknowledge any wrongdoing, instead claiming he did not recall the behaviors I described. This response eroded my confidence and left me feeling disoriented. I did express the seriousness of the harm. At one point, I told him that if such actions had been done to my own son or grandson, I felt capable of responding with anger strong enough to cause harm. Even so, I left feeling numb and disappointed in myself, as though I had not been as strong or clear as I had hoped. Looking back, I see how the setting, power dynamics, and lack of accountability shaped the encounter. What I most wanted was acknowledgment and truth.

  • Bishop - You can keep lying and pretending it did not happen. I believe that God will be the final judge on all these matters and I have my utmost confidence in Him. I still want justice in this life. But I realize not only can I not trust you, I can’t trust the nuncio. I can’t trust the church. If I continue to pursue this, I am afraid my wanting justice will turn to vengeance. And I won’t take the risk of becoming an ugly soul just because an ugly soul touched me.

Thank you for reading. Please take a moment today to pray for those who wrote these reflections - and the many, many more people who have been impacted by abuse in the Catholic Church.

~ Sara

PS: I know it has been a while since I’ve posted a Reading Roundup. Sorry about that! It’s been a crazy few months for me. I’ll post an update about that feature soon.

Please consider sharing this post to help more people connect with these important voices.

Share

item.content:encoded:
This is a difficult topic, and it stirred up many raw emotions in members of the Survivors’ Voices Panel. Others found this idea too painful or triggering to engage with and chose to pass this month—a decision I fully support. As you’ll see, those who did respond offered a wide range of perspectives. Together, their voices reflect both the complexity of the topic and the courage it takes to even consider it.

  • This is what I would say: “How do you plan to try to square this with Jesus at the final judgment? You won’t be able to lie there. He knows exactly what you have done. He knows exactly the path of destruction your actions have caused. The ‘flying monkeys’ you recruited to be your wingmen and continue the harm won’t be able to save you. Everything that has been done in the dark will be brought to the light. It won’t be just me that you harmed. It will be all the bishops and priests you took down with you to protect your lies, all that they did to try to silence me from speaking. The truth has already set me free.”

  • Thinking about having that conversation makes my stomach churn. I can imagine them sitting placidly, pretending to care, acting as though *they* were mature while I was unreasonable, throwing a tantrum… But I wish they knew that they aren’t the “experts” they pretend they are, that they knew they were harmful and abusive and toxic, that they are just as bad or worse than those they supposedly help. I wish they knew how badly they messed me up and how irrevocably they changed my life and my relationships, especially with the Church and God. I wish they knew how terrible they are—and I wish they cared. I wish I could force them to look at each instance of abuse and feel what I do. I wish they would feel like they had to make it up to me—that they would spend the rest of their lives as affected by it as I am. I wish they were terrified of going to hell, just as I so often am because of how I and my relationships with God and the Church have changed. I wish they would have to tell everyone how they hurt me. I wish *they* would have the kinds of mental, physical, and spiritual health struggles that I’ve had because of them and that they would have to go into debt to pay for professional help for it.

  • My abuser has passed away, but before he died, he had been removed from ministry by his abbot. I’d probably say something like, “I really hate what you did to yourself. One of the things that’s been the hardest to carry is that it’s my testimony that ultimately prompted your removal. I’m glad that you weren’t able to hurt anyone else, but I hate that you chose to make the choices to ruin your life, and damage so many others’, like that. I hate that that’s what it took, though I also don’t regret it. It took so many of us coming forward before anything was actually done. I forgive you... I don’t know if you repented or forgave me before you died for what you probably thought I did to you. That hurts a little. Maybe it shouldn’t, but it does.”

  • I have no desire to talk to my abusers. I don’t know why. I know I can still trigger with fear but I think I have crossed them out of my consciousness. I don’t care what they would say, their actions tell me everything. Maybe I still can’t face them. I’m not sure why I have no desire to hear what they would say, and I expect no empathy from them as I still don’t see empathy today in the Church.

  • I did actually speak briefly to the priest who abused me, and he apologized for “his sinfulness.” At that time, I know neither he nor I knew the extent of what his abuse of me as an adult woman truly meant. For me, it would mean years of therapy and spiritual counseling to recover my identity and begin repairing the image of God he so distorted, and for him, it would also mean the loss of his priesthood. Would I like to talk with him again? Sometimes I think I would like to know if he really understands what he did to me, how the power differential he had and the grooming he did made my consent impossible, how horribly corrupt it was for him to take the place of Jesus in so many ways. But truly, most of the time, I’m grateful for having had even some semblance of an apology and hope that he has received psychological and mental help for himself.

  • I would ask her, “Why did you take advantage of a vulnerable young man 10 years younger than you? What happened to you in your past to make you do such a terrible thing? Did you enjoy keeping what you described as “our little secret” from your own community? Do you understand the emotional harm and moral injury done to our marriage? You justified what you did with religious platitudes. Your prayers make me want to vomit.”

  • I honestly don’t think there’s anything I would say to my abuser. I truly doubt that he could ever be open to hearing the truth of my words. I think he is too closed off, too entrenched in the mindset of a predator, to understand anything I would want to say. And to think about receiving his response, to hear what he would say back, even to see his nonverbal cues as he listened to my words... I have already spent too much of my life considering his needs and his desires. I don’t want one more second of my life to be spent thinking about his reactions to me. I don’t need any more of his words or expressions echoing in my head.

I also want to draw special attention to this valuable comment from one survivor:

  • I am grateful to finally acknowledge and understand that he abused me. (Thank you therapy, Awake, and all the trainings I have been taking.) Having said that, I will never refer to him as “my abuser.” That is because he is not “mine” in any way. He is a person who abused me. That’s it. I will have no connection to him that the word “mine” implies. (This is solely a personal preference; I realize that others are empowered by saying “my...” and I respect that. I just don’t choose it for myself.)

I think this is a really important insight. I decided to keep the topic title as is, because it’s what I sent to the panelists to respond to, but I think this gives us all something good to consider when choosing our language.

Thank you for reading. I’ll have more reflections on this topic next month.

~ Sara

item.title: Survivors' Voices: Love
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson
item.description: One of the things I have learned from walking with abuse survivors is that even simple words can land very differently depending on a person’s past experiences. “Faith” and “hope” are among those words that can sound beautiful or painful, depending on who hears them. So is “love.” I found it very difficult to listen to words, especially in the liturgy, that had the word “love” in it because of how the word had become distorted in my perceptions of it. item.content:encoded:
One of the things I have learned from walking with abuse survivors is that even simple words can land very differently depending on a person’s past experiences. “Faith” and “hope” are among those words that can sound beautiful or painful, depending on who hears them. So is “love.”

  • I found it very difficult to listen to words, especially in the liturgy, that had the word “love” in it because of how the word had become distorted in my perceptions of it. What helped is understanding that there are different forms of “love” including abusive love, mistaken love, false love, infatuation and blind “love” - the love that takes and doesn’t give. The word love lost its meaning until I understood that love without justice is not love. “Love” can be destructive if it is centred on the ego, what the individual can get from it for their own self-satisfaction. It is abusive if it uses a person without consideration of consequences, and long-term consequences. Love is NOT a feeling. Love is a sacrament, a vow that can reveal the nature of Christ. It is NOT self-sacrifice for the sake of “forgiveness” or continuing relationships that perpetuate the abuse.

  • The effect of the abuse on my life was a sickening feeling at the word ‘love’ and an avoidance of hurt, like avoiding putting my hand onto a hot stove plate to get burnt.

  • My ability to give and receive genuine love was affected by my abuse in several ways. On the receiving side, I often felt unworthy, suspicious, or braced for the “catch” behind any tenderness, so I would either pull away or stay half-present. On the giving side, I could pour myself out in care for others, but it was frequently driven by fear, hypervigilance, or a need to manage their emotions, rather than by a relaxed, free gift of myself. Therapy, somatic work, and safe relationships have slowly helped me separate love from abuse, so that nurture, safety, and respect no longer feel foreign or undeserved.

  • One thing that has been entirely ruined for me is the imagery, as in Song of Songs, of erotic love as a metaphor for God’s relationship with the church. It’s not that I reject the place and intent of this part of the bible. But I have had to live through the perversion of those passages, and have deeply hurt by these perversions. In the aftermath of the abuse I experienced, I have learned that other outwardly “saintly” or “holy” abusers in other times and places also employed these images and passages in their deception, manipulation, and abuse.

  • Being held by my spouse as I disclosed the forty year secret of witnessing my best friend being abused was the most loving thing anyone could have done for me. It was during this moment that I knew no matter how often I share the story, I will be held in a safe embrace by the one who chose to share his life with me.

  • I describe love as understanding a person well enough to do what they need to get through painful and damaging experiences. This can be doing or saying the right thing. It can also mean helping the person just enough so as not to take away their sense of self assurance.

  • Of course, on the surface I feel the love of my wife, children, friends and others in the community. Beneath the surface, I don’t always feel that I deserve to be loved. The trauma of my childhood sexual abuse is a dark cloud over every single relationship in my life.

  • Love is a tricky word for me. My parents did not discuss or demonstrate love through hugs or words, so when my uncle began using physical affection and “I love you” to groom me at age five, I craved that attention and cooperated with his advances and molestation. The Monsignor, who was supposed to help me recover from the two years of uncle abuse, also used affection for grooming me. He spoke of Jesus’s love for me to rope me in, and Jesus’s disappointment if I did not cooperate. In the novitiate, I was told I was going to be Jesus’s wife, and I’d better learn what Jesus wanted in the bedroom if I wanted to make Him happy. That priest forced me to keep “practicing” over and over then told me that Jesus could never love or want me because of my bedroom “failures.” By the time I started dating after fleeing the novitiate, my entire idea of loving and being loved was completely twisted, which made my dating years treacherous. I found true love at age 30. We had 40 wonderful years together before he died from cancer. The last stage I learned was self-love. That required processing of the deep shame and self-blame that lurked in my subconscious mind, but I eventually mastered that, too.

  • Any experience of love in my life has been quite guarded. As a child, I longed to feel loved and cared for. So, when the priest hugged me, I welcomed it. Unfortunately, that love became shameful and even criminal. I believe it is only through the unconditional love of God that my very hardened heart has been opened. Today, I know the blessings of love and care in my life because of some remarkable, understanding, and patient people.

May we each come to understand and experience genuine love - and stand up against all the ways perversions of love are used to harm and control.

~ Sara

Please consider sharing this post to help more people connect with these important voices.

item.content:encoded:
Dear Readers,

Over the last few months, I have been reflecting on the In Spirit and Truth blog, and how I can best use my time and energies at this moment in my life.

You have probably picked up on the fact that my work with Awake continues to get busier and busier, and you may also know that I struggle with chronic illness that creates significant limitations for me.

I am currently discerning the future of this blog, and I would really appreciate hearing your thoughts about the two key elements (Survivors’ Voices posts and Reading Roundup), as well as any other feedback you want to share.

Take the Quick Poll Here

It’s only two questions, so please take just a minute to offer your thoughts!

Thank you,
Sara

item.title: The Best Collection of Survivor Stories
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson
item.description: (According to a completely biased reader)
item.content:encoded:
Hello readers,

January has been a crazy for me, with a million meetings that I put off until after the holidays, and then reviewing over 280 (!) applications for Awake’s new position. So, I wasn’t able to collect responses for a new Survivors’ Voices post this month.

However, I wanted to take a moment to point you toward what I think is a really valuable collection of stories from women and men who have experienced sexual abuse by Catholic leaders. At Awake, we have been publishing our Survivor Stories series for almost four years, and we now have 37 unique posts. I know I’m incredibly biased, but I think what we’ve done is really special.

What sets this collection apart is, first, the wide diversity of experiences included - people of a variety of ages, abuse experiences, relationships with the Catholic Church, cultural backgrounds, and more. While I certainly won’t claim that this is a representative sample, it gets a bit closer than you find in many places, and we are actively seeking to expand the collection.

Second, unlike many news pieces, these stories center the survivor’s perspective, allowing them to speak in their own words and choose the questions they want to answer. We don’t focus on the abuser or on the church hierarchy, and no story is published until the survivor approves the final version. This allows the survivor to remain in control of their narrative and the reader to really focus on the humanity of the person who is being featured.

So, if you’d like to get a more in-depth look at individual survivors’ perspectives, please check it out here:

Read Survivor Stories from Awake

Thank you for taking the time to listen.

~ Sara

PS: I want to extend tremendous thanks to Erin O’Donnell from Awake’s volunteer Leadership Team, who has worked on the majority of these posts over the years, as well as Katie Burke-Redys, who has been helping out more recently. This series is only made possible by the generous gift of their time and talents!

item.title: Survivors' Voices: Grief, Part 2
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson
item.description: Grief might seem like a strange topic for this season of joyful holidays. But I think it’s important to remember that for many people - including those who have experienced abuse - loss and sorrow are a constant undercurrent of life, no matter how many Christmas songs are playing the radio. Perhaps this is a good time to ask yourself - Who are the people in my life who might be carrying grief this time of year? And what can I do to support them? I met my abuser when I was 18, so I have a sense o…
item.content:encoded:
Grief might seem like a strange topic for this season of joyful holidays. But I think it’s important to remember that for many people - including those who have experienced abuse - loss and sorrow are a constant undercurrent of life, no matter how many Christmas songs are playing the radio.

Perhaps this is a good time to ask yourself - Who are the people in my life who might be carrying grief this time of year? And what can I do to support them?

  • I met my abuser when I was 18, so I have a sense of the young woman I was becoming before the abuse. I grieve her - the possibilities she held, the paths she might have taken, the person she might have grown into. But I also recognize that I may idealize that version of myself. Part of this healing has meant admitting that what I’m grieving isn’t only that earlier version of me, but also my (childlike) idea of what adulthood would be. Life was always going to have its crosses. I’ve had other significant burdens to carry besides the abuse. But the abuse has made everything else feel heavier, and I grieve the ways I’ve had to suffer under weight that never should have been mine in the first place.

  • Because my abuse happened in the context of a ministry in college, I’ve grieved the loss of those years. I was so overwhelmed and stressed because of the emotional/psychological parts of what was going on that I feel I missed out on a lot of the normal parts of being a college student. I envy people who can actually look back with fondness on their alma mater. I also grieve the loss of the ability to bond normally with my husband the first year or two of our marriage - I was dealing with what was most likely PTSD mixed with a hefty dose of disassociation at the time. We’re happily married 11 years later, but there was a lot of devastation and dysfunction I didn’t realize that I had to heal from. I’ve had to work actively at forgiving for the loss of those.

  • I grieve the loss of what might have been, had I not experienced the trauma of abuse. I began dealing with the abuse shortly after my husband and I were married. It put a huge strain on us emotionally and financially at a time when we were supposed to be enjoying the “honeymoon” phase of our relationship. It took several years for me to stabilize, and I deeply grieve that lost time.

  • There was the first kind of grief after my abuse, which was all-consuming, overwhelming. Every morning I would wonder how I would get through the next 7,000 minutes of the day. Five years later, the grief still shows up as a shadow, a loss, a weighted but invisible backpack that I find clinging onto my back. It can feel like lying in bed and getting the idea that maybe you left the back door wide open to the dark night: even in safe places, there can come a suspicion, a vulnerability, the reminder of a threat, no matter what you know rationally. In the story of the good samaritan, I see the wounded person watching people walk on by. Too often, this is how it feels watching the church move on in sermons and programs and plans and bishops’ meetings: not thinking to notice me on the side of the road.

  • The grief that I experienced was for the Church that I loved, that allowed a priest who had accusations from another diocese to remain in the parish (because the bishop believed the priest who said he was innocent). All the while, this same priest continued to abuse children. How can a lay person continue working for the same institution who gives lip service to safeguarding God’s children but clearly failed these children by keeping this priest near children without any oversight? I grieve for those children and for those who were impacted by the failures in the system of the protection of children.

  • The thing I grieve most about my abuse is my extreme difficulty with connecting to people emotionally. This has made me often fail to return caring feelings shown to me and has resulted in the death of many relationships.

  • Grief in regards to the clergy abuse I experienced - it would be losing my sense of safety in the Church. Up to that point, it was the safest place that I knew in the world. I lost my anchor. I wish that it was just a “one time thing.” But the bishop’s response, the reaction of other priests, the reaction and comments of those in the pew, have piled on to the experience. It isn’t just an unfortunate moment. It is a systematic failure to acknowledge truth and act in justice. What is rare is the very infrequent moment of genuine care. There is a disconnect between the actions of Church members and the Catholic Social Teaching the Church proclaims. Everything I have ever learned about what the Church is supposed to be, in reality, doesn’t exist.

  • Giving birth to my daughter brought up a lot of difficult emotions for me, because of my abuse. I struggled for a long time with the fear that I might not be able to protect her from being abused. We had always talked about having two children, but I couldn’t handle having another. The abuse took that from me, and while I know it was the right decision to make, I grieve the loss of that second child I never had.

  • Grief is a slippery slope for me. There was no grief to process before my memories surfaced. Then my energies became focused on dealing with the nightmares and flashbacks. Eventually, I got to the grief phase, where I had to think about how my life might have been different had the abuse never happened. And I must revisit that with every new memory, and there are many. With each new memory, the grief deepens. My physical, emotional, and mental health became trashed due to the abuse. I think of all the time and money I must continually spend on treatment and what I could have done with that. I am constantly battling overwhelm with tasks, relationships, activities, finances, with all of life, and that has taken its toll. I think about what life might have been like without that ton of baggage. I try to not go too far down the grief rabbit hole, because I’ve found that it just creates more depression. Instead, I try and focus on gratitude, for everything I DO have, and for my resilience and all the very close and authentic friendships I’ve developed because true and lasting healing is never done on an island.

Thank you for making space in your hearts to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), even in this season of rejoicing.

Wishing you peace and hope,
Sara

item.dc:creator: Sara Larson

item.content:encoded:
Grief was the discussion topic for our Awake Survivor Circles in November, and the conversations were both powerful and painful. While what is shared in those sacred spaces is confidential, I asked the In Spirit and Truth Survivors’ Voices Panel to share their thoughts on the topic, to give you a small peak at what grief can look like in the aftermath of abuse in the Church.

  • I didn’t understand grief for a very long time. At the worst of the trauma, I just felt sorrow that didn’t have a name. Once grief became part of my language, I allowed myself to slowly write a list of losses. It began as just a few things and now fills two typed pages - one loss per line. Years later, consequences continue to connect and other losses are added. To only see the loss is a hell that I sometimes despaired of ever being able to get through. With time, there is now a complementary list of gains beginning, and I look forward to each loss listed eventually having a victory over it.

  • Grief has been a bain on my consciousness, an unyielding presence in my now ordinary existence, wagging the finger of judgment, of failure, of blame. Grief keeps its talons firmly anchored to my memory, my heart. / Grief is my teacher. I greet her now with acceptance, acknowledging her gifts and kindness that I would not have known had this tragic experience and life circumstances not occurred, grateful now for those who nourish me, for the uniqueness of individual survivors that bring awareness that I am not alone, my heart that is being shaped and reshaped by the prayers and generosity of others. I am not the remnants of a crime scene, but an ever-evolving miracle of survival, rising now in a momentum to shine gratitude for the gift of this body, this life.

  • Grief is a very hard road to walk. It means facing the pain. “If we don’t transform our pain, we transmit it.”

  • I continue to grieve pretty deeply in the aftermath of the abuse I experienced. I grieve the loss of innocence in my view of the Church, of clergy, and of religious. I grieve the loss of the joyful enthusiasm for the traditions, liturgies, prayer, sacramentals that I used to have. I grieve the loss of my favorite ways of praying and listening to God, which I can no longer trust and are now often too triggering. I grieve the loss of a sense of being loved, with a personal calling and vocation from God. I grieve the loss of trust in my own ability to discern well, to trust myself and my gut, and even sometimes to know what is real and what’s not. I grieve the way the abuse I experienced has caused me to hate myself and to think I’m stupid. I grieve that I am now constantly afraid of others “finding out” that my abuser was right about me and my stupidity, immaturity, irresponsibility, and incompetency. I grieve that I now can’t handle having others even look at me or my body without being terrified and ashamed, without wanting to hide. I grieve the loss of my mental health and of the ability to trust others easily. And I especially grieve the profound loss of a sense of connection, safety, and belovedness when it comes to my relationship with God: I no longer trust him or feel safe with him or even feel very close to him anymore, I no longer see him as gentle or loving or as someone who cares about and will protect me. That relationship used to be (and to some extent still is) the center and most important part of my life and—although I clearly grieve many things deeply—I think that’s where the grief hits the hardest.

  • So, ‘which’ grief should I reflect on? The grief of what I experienced during - and in the wake of - the abusive behavior, or the grief surrounding the losses to which it led... my children and ultimately my grandchildren? My reputation? My well-being and self-image? Just today I chose to share my story with a therapist I’ve been working with for about a year and a half, because after 11 years I finally accepted that I have lost my children (and subsequently, my grandchildren). I realize that I have not addressed the core issues resulting from what I experienced and how it impacts me today. Because 25 years is long enough to grieve - not just what happened, and not just the obvious consequences, but also the self-loathing, self-blame, and shame that has seeped into the deepest parts of my psyche.

  • We understand it is a colossal act of courage for any adult to separate from an abusive relationship to protect themselves and heal. I was a child, and I had to end my own abusive relationship with the priest in order to protect myself from further harm. Nobody helped me. Not my parents. Not any other adult. Nobody. I grieve the horrible isolation and deep soul crushing despair I felt. I was still a child, and I carry this wound with me still to this day.

  • The monastery sent a representative to me when I reported my abuse, and she tried her absolute darndest to get me to say I forgave my abuser and thought he could go back into ministry. She gave me the pretty distinct impression that whether he got to reenter ministry depended on what I said in that meeting. I didn’t give her what she wanted, and from what I’ve heard, he was kept out of ministry and died a few years later at a relatively young age (in his 50s) from a heart issue soon after, possibly caused by emotional turmoil and stress. I know that his actions brought him there, but I still feel grief and a burden over that decision being put on me. Even when someone has done wrong to you, and ultimately brought pain onto themselves, it can be a heavy thing for your word to be what drives the final nail into the coffin. Whether it should be or not, that’s still an ache.

  • I do experience grief related to my abuse. The losses I grieve include my sense of safety, trust, and a portion of my youthful innocence. At different stages of my life, this grief has shown up in various ways—sometimes as sadness, anger, or difficulty connecting deeply with certain institutions or people. Over time, the grief has shifted; while its intensity has softened, it sometimes re-emerges with significant events or anniversaries. Today, I recognize grief’s presence but also find that compassion and reflection have helped me integrate it into my story, rather than letting it dominate my life.

Thank you for listening to both the sorrow and the wisdom in these voices. I will share more survivors’ reflections on this topic next month.

Peace,
Sara

PS: If you have experienced abuse by a Catholic leader and would like to share your own thoughts on this or future topics, I would be grateful to include your perspective. You can find information about joining the Survivors’ Voices Panel here: An Invitation for Survivors.

Sharing these posts with friends is a great way to amplify the voices of survivors!

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to your October 2025 In Spirit and Truth Reading Roundup!

For those who are new here (welcome everyone!), this Reading Roundup is a collection of the latest news and commentary on abuse and institutional betrayal in the Catholic Church, with a particular focus on the United States. Please note that I highlight articles from a variety of sources and perspectives, and inclusion here does not mean that I agree with everything in a given article, only that I think it’s worth reading. If you only have time to read a few pieces this month, I recommend you start with those in bold below.

Pope Leo XIV

  • Pope meets with global group of clergy abuse survivors to talk zero tolerance + Leo XIV meets global survivor advocacy group in Vatican

  • Pope Leo critic now says her lawyer might have had a secret agenda + Victim in abuse case used against the Pope speaks out, confirming that her lawyer exploited her

Vatican News

  • Vatican report calls for reparations for sex abuse victims and tougher sanctions for abusers + What’s in the Vatican’s 2nd global child protection report? + Complete report here

  • Group defining crime of spiritual abuse making good progress, cardinal says

  • Vatican announces selection of judges in Rupnik trial

International News

  • Argentina: Bishop Zanchetta released on parole

  • England: Abuse survivors in driving seat of new Church initiative

  • Peru: Bishop accused of having 17 lovers exposed by cleaning lady

  • Portugal: Victims protest inaction from Portuguese bishops on financial compensation

  • Uruguay: Ex-priest accused of abusing 30 boys finally detained after 18 years

U.S. News

  • Illinois: Suburban woman accusing Catholic priest of sexual misconduct says: ‘I feel betrayed’

  • Indiana: Notre Dame announces investigation into alleged sexual misconduct by dorm hall priest

  • Minnesota: Charges say Catholic priest in central Minnesota sexually abused woman he was advising

  • New York: Citing ‘Credible’ Sexual Misconduct Allegation, Diocese Removes Basilica of Our Lady of Perpetual Help Deacon From Ministry

  • Vermont: For Vermont survivors of orphanage abuse, the restorative justice process is over. The journey is not.

  • Washington: Washington will not require priests to report child abuse disclosed in confession

  • Washington: Spokane priest accused of sexual misconduct, misuse of funds

  • Wisconsin: 4 years into faith leader investigation, Wisconsin DOJ has received over 300 reports

Reflection, Opinion, and Analysis

  • When the Mother Superior puts the stockings on the novice

  • Balancing rights: Why the ‘McKnight plan’ is in line with Leo’s priorities

  • Survivor impact statement by Colleen Garbarini

  • The Next Clergy Sex Abuse Scandal Is Taking Place Right Now—in Bankruptcy Court

  • Why the Traditional vs. Liberal Catholic Divide is Enabling Sexual Abuse

Thank you all for reading, and for caring about this important issue. I’ll be back in November with more survivor reflections.

With gratitude,
Sara

item.title: Survivors' Voices: Healing, Part 2
item.dc:creator: Sara Larson
item.description: One of the things I appreciate most about the ISAT Survivors’ Voices panelists is their thought-provoking honesty about words and ideas that are often discussed only at a surface level. item.content:encoded:
One of the things I appreciate most about the ISAT Survivors’ Voices panelists is their thought-provoking honesty about words and ideas that are often discussed only at a surface level. The reflections for this month are prime example of that, and I’m honored to share them with you today.

(If you missed the first installment on this topic, you can find it here: Survivors' Voices: Healing, Part 1.)

  • I used to have this idea of healing that I would look and act like someone who had not been through trauma. Someone who made friends easily, who was easily lovable, who had a fit body, who didn’t struggle with depression or anxiety, who didn’t self-harm. I wanted to be someone who wasn’t me. I wanted to be a person who had never experienced sexual trauma, whose innocence was not stripped away at such a young age. As the years went on, I realized that person was never going to exist. I had to grieve that reality. Slowly, my idea of healing has evolved. I now strive to slowly improve my life and to be a better wife, mother, and friend. I work on what it means to have boundaries and self-care. I try to practice being a loving presences to others and also to myself. I doubt I will ever be completely free of these wounds, but my life can still be good.

  • Healing has been an important concept for me as a survivor, a critical goalpost that anchors my journey. I remember how hopeful it seemed when I learned the concept of post-traumatic resilience–here was something I could aim for, the idea that as a survivor I might even one day have a kind of deep resilience despite the trauma. I can see evidence of a growing resilience, which I notice both in my internal reactions to daily events, and in how I can be present for others who are facing trauma. Part of healing, though, has been to filter a lot of noise – others’ ideas about healing and forgiveness, how I should feel, and whether or when I would be “back to normal” (which they believe includes returning to a naive state of belief in authority and piety in the church). This constant filtering means it takes me a lot of extra, invisible time and energy to figure out what’s really true, and what I want and need in a given moment and season.

  • Healing has been an interesting journey. The most unexpected part of it is realizing that things I was struggling with and thought were unrelated to the abuse suddenly improved immensely once I started facing the abuse and working through it. So much of ourselves is intertwined.

  • It’s been frustrating that I don’t feel like my particular wound is one I can share in most popular avenues for healing in the Church. I’ll hear about a healing retreat, even one centered on healing from sexual wounds, and have the distinct feeling that such things aren’t going to bear fruit for me - I’d cause scandal to fellow retreatants or have the retreat director or priest on staff freaked out by what I’m carrying and they wouldn’t be able to help. Or else I’ll attract another predator or someone well meaning but inept and get hurt again. Awake’s offerings on this front have been wonderful, but I still wish I didn’t feel like an outcast from the “normal” avenues for these things.

  • I have been thinking about what my life feels like now. It is the sense of going through the motions and actions of the Church, feeling like a pin ball in a Church pin ball machine. Fearful of what “lever” I’m going to get “whacked” by today. What priest is going to realize I’m a survivor and be too “uncomfortable” to have me participate in anything. What Catholic employer is concerned, “What if a bishop realizes we have an survivor working here?” And I miss out on work/opportunities or lose a job I’ve been competently doing without issue. Healing would the chance for me to finally be not fearful. To be seen, heard, and supported. The abuse and resulting trauma isn’t my identity. Beloved child of God is my identity. Healing is when the Church sees and acts on my true identity, not my history of my lived experience.

  • There’s no “healed.” This trauma will be with me for the rest of my life. The grooming took places over years, the abuse over minutes/hours, and now decades lie ahead, maybe as many as six or seven of them, where I have to learn how to live with the impact of the abuse on my body and soul. On one hand, it’s terrifying to acknowledge that this journey will never be in the past tense, only ever present and ongoing. On the other hand, once I acknowledge that this journey is never-ending, I can release myself from the burden of not being at some unattainable finish line.

  • We call it closure, but what we really crave is a physiological exhale.

    The body wants proof the danger has passed.

  • I’m really torn about “healing” as a concept, at least as it pertains to what happened to me. I was abused in the context of a very vulnerable and profound gift of self to Jesus. That gift matters deeply to me and is sometimes the only thing I can hold onto as proof when I feel like I don’t really love Jesus anymore. Any other gifts of self I’ve given seem to pale in comparison. But being abused in that context also shattered everything about my identity, my spirituality, my relationships with God and others. If “healing” means moving on and not being affected by what happened anymore, then I’m not sure I want—nor will ever really achieve—healing. To move on and no longer be affected would then seem to minimize or erase the gift I gave and I simply can’t do that—it *has* to have meant something, it *has* to have been real and important and even sacrificial in some way. Otherwise I have nothing left to hold onto.

  • I know I will be healed when I can embrace this cross, as Christ embraced His, and raise my head, look to the Father and say with Jesus: “Forgive them, Father, they know not what they do.” I know I will never reach this without the Sacraments of confession and communion. I turn to Our Lady of Sorrows in prayer to guide me to this healing.

  • Healing is acknowledging and receiving acknowledgement as to how I was hurt, and the hurt and damage done both to me and to others with whom my life was closely connected. It is being allowed to stay in my grief and anger as long as I need to, so that I can work through the issues for myself, in my own time. I started by naming my pain, then praying for the person who hurt me. Healing is like learning to walk with a leg amputated. Pain takes time to heal. The sense of loss remains. Even with the healing process, the damage is there, and the work in learning to walk again with one leg is hard work. I have had to reconsider all that I once held as true, as certain words have lost their meaning. I needed to learn to speak my truth. After suffering all these years, I started questioning my assumptions and the values and principles I uphold, while holding onto the ethical questions to find my own healing. My anger helps me to refuse to accept what was unacceptable, grieve my losses, and voice my pain. Thank you for this healing space, Sara.

If you’re interested in an in-depth exploration of three more survivors’ perspectives on healing, check out this summary and recording of Awake’s recent online event: Listening to Survivors: What Has Helped My Healing Journey.

Peace,
Sara

Would you consider sharing this post on social media or with someone you think might be interested? I would love to have more people hear these important voices.

Share

item.content:encoded:
In preparation for Awake's upcoming virtual survivor panel on "What Has Helped My Healing Journey" (sign up here to join us live this Thursday or receive the video by email), I have been thinking a lot about healing - and what that word means to different people. I thought it would be valuable to hear reflections from a variety of survivors on this topic.

Note: As my work with Awake gets busier and busier, I'm going to experiment with a change to the flow of Survivors' Voices posts. Instead of two posts in one month on the same topic, I am going to publish those posts over two months. In this case, that will mean one post on healing in mid-September and another in mid-October. I hope this will be a good way to allow you to still hear from the voices of survivors, while lessening my work load here a little. Now, on to the reflections:

  • I used to think that “healing” meant being able to put the abuse completely behind me so I could forget about it and get on with life like it never happened. As more and more additional memories kept surfacing, I realized that the entire healing process was a journey. Healing for me has involved numerous layers of processing, including working through my own denial that any of it could ever have happened, then working through excruciating layers of shame, self-blame, guilt and anger that were far more intense than I ever could have anticipated. The tentacles of the abuse invaded my emotions, my mental state, my body and my soul, all of which I’ve had to address. It has taken several years to reach a point where I have been able to find forgiveness and peace, and even then, the surfacing of additional memories creates a need for more work. A huge accomplishment was when all my hard work resulted in fewer and shorter periods of flashbacks and nightmares, and ultimately, increasing periods of calm and peace, and an expanding capacity to also experience happiness and joy.

  • Healing to me means living as positively as possible. I think healing means different things to different survivors, and each person should be allowed their own interpretation. I consider myself healing when I keep learning and connecting with other survivors.

  • Healing from Catholic clergy abuse has been an intimate and deeply personal journey for me, shaped by a mosaic of relationships, faith practices, and courageous acts of vulnerability. My pathway forward began with sharing my story—a process that I postponed for decades out of fear, shame, and the loneliness that comes with carrying such pain alone. When I finally found the courage to speak, and was met with genuine compassion and attentive listening from friends, therapists, and spiritual guides, I discovered that this act of disclosure could transform my pain into real connection and foster the relief of being truly seen and heard. In those moments, I felt God’s grace present and active through the supportive presence of those who walked the path of healing alongside me.

  • For me, healing came unnoticed. I was not horribly traumatized, so a need to heal was not on my radar screen. When I reported, it was more to assure that my abuser was included, not because it meant much to me. However, I realized I was not afraid to stand up and say my truth. More importantly I also recognized that I had forgiven him for being abusive , but also me from the feeling that I somehow was at fault. So I have always equated healing with my forgiveness of a naive, immature teen who was in over her head.

  • Not holding back any longer, finally telling my wife my story of childhood sexual abuse, and her warm and loving reaction is healing to me. Since we are active parishioners, I felt it was best to tell our pastor my story. He heard the depth of my sadness and pain. This dialogue was healing to me. Coming forward and telling my story to my diocese, and feeling heard, believed, and valued, was healing to me. Going to therapy was healing to me. Accepting victim assistance outreach services over the past 19 years, and still to this day, is healing to me. For me, healing has never been a solitary act - I cannot heal from my wounds alone. I am grateful for the many people who accompany me on my healing journey.

Thank you for listening. I will share more survivors’ reflections on this topic next month.

Peace,
Sara

PS: If you have experienced abuse by a Catholic leader and would like to share your own thoughts on this or future topics, I would be grateful to include your perspective. You can find information about joining the Survivors’ Voices Panel here: An Invitation for Survivors.

Sharing these posts with friends is a great way to amplify the voices of survivors!
